content.p: Jeffrey Epstein was a New York money manager who used his wealth, his homes and a chain of paid recruiters to sexually abuse girls, many of them high school students, over a period of years. Police in Palm Beach, Florida, uncovered the abuse in 2005. Federal prosecutors drafted a 60-count indictment against him, and then, in a secret agreement, let him plead guilty instead to two state prostitution charges. He served less than 13 months in a county jail, much of it on daytime work release, and returned to a life among the rich and famous.

A decade later, reporting by the Miami Herald put the case back in front of the public, and in July 2019 federal prosecutors in New York charged him with sex trafficking of minors. A month later he was found hanged in his cell in a Manhattan jail. His death, ruled a suicide, ended the prosecution but not the case. His longtime companion Ghislaine Maxwell was convicted of sex trafficking in 2021, banks that served him paid hundreds of millions of dollars to his victims, and a law passed in 2025 forced the government to publish millions of pages of its files on him.

Epstein left college without a degree, taught for a time at Manhattan's elite Dalton School, and passed through the investment bank Bear Stearns before setting up his own advisory firm. Al Jazeera, drawing on documents released in 2026, reported that he met Leslie Wexner, the billionaire founder of L Brands, the company behind Victoria's Secret, by 1986. Five years later Wexner gave him full power of attorney, which let Epstein act for him in almost everything: writing cheques, hiring people, taking loans and dealing in property. A 1998 agreement put Wexner's townhouse at 9 East 71st Street in Manhattan formally under Epstein's control, and it became his New York base. In 1996 he moved his firm to the US Virgin Islands.

Wexner has said he cut ties with Epstein around 2007 after discovering that Epstein had "misappropriated vast sums of money from me and my family". "I was naive, foolish, and gullible to put any trust in Jeffrey Epstein," he said in 2026. "He was a con man." He has never been charged with any crime. The relationship, and the wealth and standing it brought, gave Epstein access to politicians, academics and business leaders. Photographs of him with famous and powerful people hung on his walls.

In March 2005 the parents of a 14-year-old girl told the Palm Beach police that Epstein had paid her for a massage at his mansion. The investigation that followed, according to the Justice Department's later review, found that he used personal assistants to recruit girls to give him massages, which in many instances led to sexual activity. Julie K. Brown, the Miami Herald reporter who later told the story, described the pattern: a girl would hear from a friend that she could earn a couple of hundred dollars giving a rich man a massage, be taken into a darkened room where he lay on a table, be abused, and be paid. Then she would be offered money to bring other girls. "That was sort of the pyramid scheme that he created," Brown said.

Many of the girls came from difficult homes, some from foster care, and Brown said Epstein studied their weaknesses and promised to help them become models or go to school. Michelle Licata, a straight-A student who went to his house once hoping to earn money for Christmas presents, told Brown that her life unravelled afterwards. Courtney Wild said she went to him from the age of 14 and spent years trying to numb the memory.

The lead detective, Joe Recarey, pursued the case with great dedication, Brown said. In May 2006 police officials signed papers seeking several counts of unlawful sexual activity with a minor against him. The state attorney for Palm Beach County, Barry Krischer, instead took the unusual step of sending the case to a grand jury, which in July 2006 indicted Epstein on a single count of soliciting prostitution. The police chief and the detective, convinced that the charge did not reflect what he had done, took the case to the FBI.

An assistant US attorney in Florida opened a federal case with the knowledge of the US Attorney, R. Alexander Acosta. With two FBI agents she found more victims, and in May 2007 she gave her supervisors a draft 60-count indictment. Instead of approving it, the office met Epstein's lawyers on 31 July 2007 and offered to drop its investigation if he pleaded guilty to state charges, served at least two years, registered as a sex offender and agreed to a way for victims to claim damages.

The deal that was signed on 24 September 2007 was softer. Epstein would plead guilty in state court to the solicitation charge and to procuring minors for prostitution, which would require him to register as a sex offender, and would serve 18 months in the county jail followed by a year of house arrest. In return the US Attorney's office agreed not to prosecute him federally in its district, or four named co-conspirators, or "any potential co-conspirators". The victims were not told about the deal or consulted before it was signed, and letters sent to them afterwards described the federal investigation as still open.

Epstein's lawyers then spent nine months trying to change terms they had already negotiated, and to have the whole agreement set aside, appealing to senior officials in Washington. Private investigators working for his side followed some of the girls and their families, Brown said, as well as the lead detective. On 23 June 2008 the office of the Deputy Attorney General refused to intervene, and on 30 June Epstein pleaded guilty. He was sent to a minimum-security Palm Beach County facility. By October he was spending 12 hours a day on work release at a "Florida Science Foundation" he had recently incorporated, located in the West Palm Beach office of one of his lawyers. With time off for good behaviour he served less than 13 months, and on 22 July 2009 he was released to a year of home detention.

A victim identified as Jane Doe went to federal court in July 2008 claiming that the government had broken the Crime Victims' Rights Act by keeping the deal from them. Eleven years later, in February 2019, a judge agreed that it had. A November 2020 review by the Justice Department's Office of Professional Responsibility found that Acosta had not committed professional misconduct and found no evidence that his decision was driven by corruption or by Epstein's wealth, status or associations. It concluded, however, that resolving the case through the agreement "constitutes poor judgment", and that the victims "were not treated with the forthrightness and sensitivity expected by the Department."

Epstein settled many of the civil suits brought by his victims and resumed his lavish life with little press attention. In 2009 Virginia Roberts Giuffre sued him, alleging that he and Maxwell had arranged for her to have sexual encounters with powerful men. Her later public accusations against Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, then Prince Andrew, created a crisis for the British royal family; he denied them and later settled her lawsuit for an undisclosed sum. Giuffre died in Australia in April 2025. All the men she named have denied her allegations.

In 2017 President Donald Trump nominated Acosta as Labor Secretary, and he was questioned only briefly about Epstein at his confirmation hearing. Around that time Brown began looking again at a case she called a horrendous miscarriage of justice that everyone seemed to have forgotten. She and the visual journalist Emily Michot identified 80 women who had been abused and persuaded several to speak on the record. The Herald published "Perversion of Justice" on 28 November 2018. Within days the FBI and federal prosecutors in Manhattan had opened a new investigation.

On the evening of 6 July 2019 Epstein was arrested at Teterboro Airport in New Jersey, aboard his private jet, which had just landed from Paris. Two days later the US Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Geoffrey Berman, announced a two-count indictment for sex trafficking and conspiracy. It alleged that from at least 2002 to 2005 Epstein had abused dozens of girls, some as young as 14, at his Manhattan mansion and his Palm Beach estate, paying them hundreds of dollars in cash and paying some to recruit others. "The alleged behavior shocks the conscience," Berman said.

Agents searching the Manhattan house found what prosecutors described as a vast collection of lewd photographs of young-looking women or girls, some in a locked safe on discs labelled by hand. Arguing that he should be kept in jail, prosecutors wrote: "The defendant, a registered sex offender, is not reformed, he is not chastened, he is not repentant." Epstein pleaded not guilty. His lawyer, Reid Weingarten, called the case "a re-do" of conduct already settled by the Florida agreement. New York prosecutors said that agreement did not bind them. The judge ordered him held. On 12 July 2019 Acosta resigned as Labor Secretary.

Epstein spent 36 days at the Metropolitan Correctional Center in Manhattan. About two weeks before his death he was found with injuries to his neck in what jail officials treated as a suicide attempt, and he was put on suicide watch for 31 hours. He was supposed to share a cell, but his cellmate left for a court hearing and was not replaced. On the night of 9 August the two officers assigned to his unit, both working overtime, failed to make the required checks every 30 minutes. They were sleeping and shopping online, prosecutors later said, and falsified the records. He was found hanged with bed linen at about 6:30 a.m. on 10 August. The city's chief medical examiner ruled his death a suicide, and the indictment was dismissed.

In June 2023 the Justice Department's inspector general, Michael Horowitz, blamed a "combination of negligence, misconduct and outright job performance failures" for giving one of the most notorious prisoners in the federal system the chance to take his own life. Epstein had been left with excess sheets and clothing, allowed to sleep on the floor and to make an unmonitored phone call the night before he died, and nearly all the cameras on his unit were not recording. Horowitz found no evidence of foul play and nothing to contradict the FBI's conclusion that no crime was involved in the death. The two officers admitted falsifying records and avoided prison under a deal with prosecutors. Officials announced in 2021 that the jail would close.

Doubts persist. Epstein's brother, Mark Epstein, has argued that the death needed deeper investigation, and in October 2026 a professor of forensic medicine, Michael Freeman, said he would present an analysis of the autopsy records in London in November. He pointed out that no photographs of the body were taken at the scene and that the ligature was not preserved. "The death can only be a suicide or a homicide, and the lecture will describe the weight (of) evidence for both explanations," he said, declining to give his conclusion in advance. In May 2026 a federal judge ordered the release of an apparent suicide note connected with the July 2019 incident, which Epstein's former cellmate, Nicholas Tartaglione, said he had found in a book. It includes the phrase "time to say goodbye".

In August 2019 more than a dozen of Epstein's victims spoke at a court hearing about what he had done to them. Ghislaine Maxwell was charged in July 2020 with helping recruit and abuse his victims and was convicted after a month-long trial in December 2021. She is serving a 20-year sentence and continues to deny wrongdoing.

Victims also pursued the institutions around him. In 2023 Deutsche Bank agreed to pay $75 million and JPMorgan Chase $290 million to settle claims that they had kept Epstein as a client despite warning signs. The judge in the JPMorgan case, Jed Rakoff, noted that the bank had filed suspicious activity reports about Epstein's accounts as early as 2002. "We all now understand that Epstein's behavior was monstrous," the bank said, calling any association with him a mistake that it regretted.

Epstein's friendships with famous men, among them Trump and former President Bill Clinton, kept him at the centre of political argument. Both have denied any knowledge of his crimes. In February 2025 Attorney General Pam Bondi suggested that an Epstein "client list" was on her desk. On 7 July 2025 the Justice Department said there was no such list and that no more files would be released. The backlash, much of it from Trump's own supporters, led Congress to pass the Epstein Files Transparency Act in November 2025, which Trump signed on 19 November.

The department began releasing records in December and, after missing the deadline, published more than 3 million pages, 2,000 videos and 180,000 images on 30 January 2026, about half of the roughly six million pages it had collected. Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche said the department had not protected anyone. Reporters found that the files contained emails and invitations involving many prominent people, which NPR noted were not in themselves evidence of wrongdoing; that some documents were almost entirely blacked out; and that in places victims' names and photographs had been left visible. A group of 20 women who say Epstein abused them responded: "This is not over."
As of early 2026, none of the people named or pictured in the released files had been charged with any crime, apart from Maxwell.
